hooks.text: Panicked citizens in 1910 scrambled to buy gas masks and anti-comet pills.
Why did panicked citizens scramble to buy gas masks in 1910?
A harmless space traveler forced panicked citizens to buy gas masks.

title: The Comet That Sold Gas Masks and Fake Pills
description: In 1910, the detection of cyanogen gas in Halley's Comet sent Earth into a panic, sparking massive sales of gas masks and quack remedies.

beats.text: Panicked citizens in 1910 scrambled to buy gas masks and anti-comet pills.
beats.visual: Historical photo of people wearing early twentieth-century gas masks, 1910

beats.text: The bizarre panic began when astronomers detected toxic cyanogen gas in a comet's tail.
beats.visual: Illustration of a comet with a bright tail, 1910

beats.text: Sensationalized media reports quickly convinced the public that this toxic gas would wipe out all life.
beats.visual: Newspaper clipping from 1910 warning about Halley's Comet

beats.text: The celestial culprit was Halley's Comet, a famous visitor returning every seventy-four to seventy-nine years.
beats.visual: Bayeux Tapestry section depicting Halley's Comet, 1066

beats.text: Even writer Mark Twain predicted his own death during this 1910 passage, passing away that April.
But modern space probes revealed the terrifying toxic threat is actually a harmless, peanut-shaped ball of ice.
beats.visual: Giotto probe photograph of Halley's Comet nucleus, 1986

beats.text: Its giant fifteen-kilometer nucleus is blacker than coal, reflecting only about four percent of sunlight.
beats.visual: Giotto space probe composite image of comet Halley nucleus, 1986

beats.text: This dark traveler safely returns around 2061, far too distant to make panicked citizens scramble.
beats.visual: Wide shot of the Very Large Telescope under a starry night sky, 2020

better_than_last: Applied a high-tension mystery structure and an active mystery statement hook to prevent early viewer drop-off.
